task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: shaper role subtyping by play-type initiation mix
methodological_questions: How to define cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers from play-by-play initiation data?
How to measure portability ('travels better') for a shaper role?
What unit of analysis and sample size are available for comparing mover subtypes?
How to control for confounding player attributes and team context?
Can a between-group difference be detected with n=24 shaper movers?

historical_evidence.finding: Lineups covering all three core roles (including shaper) did not score more per possession than accumulation of role counts, after controlling for talent. Result: beta=+0.42 pts/100, p=0.595; MDE80=2.19 pts/100. Adequately powered null result.
Shaper is a distinct role; lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team and is separable from talent and role counts. Gate passed.
The travel x fit framework (additive vs irrelevant mover profiles) predicts embedded minutes and net rating in holdout splits. Additive > irrelevant in 96% of splits for net rating.
Travel forecast (portability) significantly predicts mover embedded minutes and net rating (corr 0.20, AUC 0.60) in 230 movers. Additive > irrelevant in 98% of splits.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Confirmatory test of lineup role coverage (including shaper) on points per possession
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null result; estimate +0.42 pts/100, MDE80=2.19 pts/100. Shows role effects at lineup level are small and hard to detect even with large possession samples.

evidence_establishes: Travel (role portability) metrics are validated and can predict mover outcomes with moderate signal ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Shaper is a distinct, separable role with low correlation with talent ([prior work][prior work]).
Role-related hypotheses in this project are often underpowered for small true effects; large, well-powered studies have required 0.4M+ possessions and still produced null results (FAM:[prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether cut-heavy shapers differ from drive-heavy shapers in portability.
The reliability or optimal threshold for classifying a shaper as cut-heavy vs drive-heavy.
The magnitude of any differential travel effect, nor whether it is materially large enough to detect with n=24 movers.
own_inferences: n=24 shaper movers over four seasons is very small; a between-group comparison will have low power unless the effect is implausibly large (e.g., >1.5 SD difference).
Classification into cut-heavy/drive-heavy from limited player-season possessions could be noisy, causing attenuation and further power loss.

Confounders like player size, athleticism, previous team system, and offensive role likely correlate with play-type profile and portability, making causal attribution difficult even with adequate power.
uncertainties: The actual distribution of cut and drive initiation shares among the 24 shaper movers; some groups may be extremely small.
Whether the travel metric can be computed consistently for all shaper movers without lookahead leakage or look-back bias across partial seasons.
The true effect size—no prior study has examined this specific comparison, so plausible effect sizes are unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence confirms that a validated travel framework exists and that role subtyping is feasible, but does not alter the severe sample-size constraint. Even without prior work, n=24 would likely be deemed insufficient; [prior work] reinforces the prevalence of low power in role studies.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 24 shaper mover units are available across all seasons; a between-group test likely has power <0.3 for moderate effects.
Play-type profile (cut vs drive heavy) is correlated with other player and team attributes that also affect portability.
The number of cut-heavy or drive-heavy shapers may be too small to reliably estimate group means.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work validates the travel framework and confirms shaper as a measurable role, but does not test the cut-vs-drive subtype hypothesis.

risks.text: n=24 movers provides insufficient power to detect likely between-group differences; standard errors will be large.
Player attributes (size, athleticism, prior team system) are correlated with both play-type profile and portability, threatening causal interpretation.
After splitting shapers into cut-heavy and drive-heavy, each group may have very few movers, yielding unstable estimates.
Defining cut-heavy vs drive-heavy from limited possession samples (per player per season) may be unreliable, adding measurement error.
Movers are a selected subset of players; results may not generalise to shapers who do not switch teams.
If multiple thresholds or alternative subtyping rules are explored post-hoc, false positive probability increases.

design.estimand: Difference in mean travel portability (a pre-validated forecast of destination embedded minutes or net rating, computed from source-team play-type profile) between cut-heavy and drive-heavy shaper movers, controlling for prior talent, usage, and age.
design.unit: A shaper mover (player who changes teams from one season to the next), where shaper is defined as low-usage, positive residual influence.
design.sample: All shaper movers from 2022-23 → 2023-24, 2023-24 → 2024-25, and 2024-25 → 2025-26, using complete regular-season data for source and destination years; n≈24. Exclude rookies and players with fewer than 100 possessions in the source season.
design.power: Assuming n=24, a two-group comparison with balanced groups would have ~50% power to detect a ~1.2 SD difference at alpha=0.05 (two-sided). Realistic effect sizes are likely much smaller, implying power <0.2.
design.controls: Prior talent (leave-one-out APM or equivalent), prior usage, age, source-team play-type diversity, and destination team fixed effects (if sample allows) to reduce confounding.
design.falsification: Repeat analysis using alternative shaper subtyping (e.g., spot-up-heavy vs others) that should show no differential travel; if a similar pattern appears, the method is suspect.
design.multiplicity: Pre-specify a single binary cut-vs-drive classification (proportion CUT > proportion DRIVE) and a single portability outcome. No exploratory subgroup analyses without adjustment.
design.decision_rule: Primary outcome: travel forecast score. Report OLS regression of travel on a cut-heavy indicator with robust standard errors, pre-registered one-sided alternative (cut-heavy > drive-heavy). Declare support only if p<0.05 and effect direction matches hypothesis. Given low power, also report MDE and confidence intervals.
design.data_version: Play-by-play and derived possession data snapshot as of 2026-08-08, using all available seasons as described.
